About this citation

A short legal-philosophical opinion on the relation between the Law and philosophy. It has no chapter divisions, so the archive cites a described section rather than a number.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to The Decisive Treatise, on the Law’s call to reflection (Butterworth) and files it under Islamic Philosophy.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Averroes

Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198) served as qāḍī and physician in al-Andalus while producing the most influential Arabic commentaries on Aristotle. In the Decisive Treatise he argues that the Law itself obliges demonstrative reflection; in The Incoherence of the Incoherence he answers al-Ghazālī’s attack on the philosophers.

How to read this passage

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, power, inquiry.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The Law has urged us to observe beings…”?

“The Law has urged us to observe beings…” comes from Fasl al-maqal (The Decisive Treatise), on the Law’s call to reflection (Butterworth) (c. 1179–1180 CE), attributed to Averroes.

What does Averroes mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, power, inquiry.
